bibl.title: Simple statistical identification and removal of contaminant sequences in marker-gene and metagenomics data

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: contaminant DNA in marker-gene and metagenomic sequencing - sequences that are in the data and not in the sample - and how to identify them without knowing in advance what they are
span.quote: However, the accuracy of marker-gene and metagenomic sequencing (MGS) is limited in practice by several processes that introduce contaminants—DNA sequences not truly present in the sampled community.

span.label: whether contaminant sequences can be separated from true community members de novo, using only statistical patterns already present in a standard sequencing run
span.quote: Decontam implements two simple de novo classification methods based on widely reproduced signatures of external contamination: (1) Sequences from contaminating taxa are likely to have frequencies that inversely correlate with sample DNA concentration and (2) sequences from contaminating taxa are likely to have higher prevalence in control samples than in true samples.

span.label: decontam: two independent classifiers built on two reproduced signatures of contamination - inverse correlation with DNA concentration, and higher prevalence in negative controls - released as an R package
span.quote: Decontam implements two simple de novo classification methods based on widely reproduced signatures of external contamination: (1) Sequences from contaminating taxa are likely to have frequencies that inversely correlate with sample DNA concentration and (2) sequences from contaminating taxa are likely to have higher prevalence in control samples than in true samples.

span.label: method
span.quote: Decontam implements two simple de novo classification methods based on widely reproduced signatures of external contamination: (1) Sequences from contaminating taxa are likely to have frequencies that inversely correlate with sample DNA concentration and (2) sequences from contaminating taxa are likely to have higher prevalence in control samples than in true samples.

span.label: contamination that survives good laboratory practice and is invisible to the quality control usually used to detect it, biasing hardest exactly where biomass is lowest and the claims are most contested
span.quote: Contamination is often assumed to be absent if control samples do not yield a band on an agarose gel. However, band-less samples can generate non-negligible numbers of sequencing reads, suggesting that gel-based quality control is insufficient.

span.label: a two-component mixture model of contaminant and sample DNA, turned into two score statistics and a user-set classification threshold, validated on an oral dataset, a dilution series and two published low-biomass studies
span.term: a two-component mixture model of contaminant and sample DNA, turned into two score statistics and a user-set classification threshold, validated on an oral dataset, a dilution series and two published low-biomass studies
span.quote: Let total sample DNA (T) be a mixture of two components (T = C + S): contaminating DNA (C) present in uniform concentration across samples and true sample DNA (S) present in varying concentration across samples.

span.label: contaminant DNA enters at roughly constant absolute concentration while sample DNA varies, so as a proportion of the total the contaminant's frequency falls as sample concentration rises - a slope of -1 in log space against a slope of 0
span.quote: Let total sample DNA (T) be a mixture of two components (T = C + S): contaminating DNA (C) present in uniform concentration across samples and true sample DNA (S) present in varying concentration across samples.

span.label: with no competing sample DNA, a negative control's sequencing capacity is available to whatever contaminant is present, so contaminants are detected in a larger fraction of controls than of true samples
span.quote: Decontam implements two simple de novo classification methods based on widely reproduced signatures of external contamination: (1) Sequences from contaminating taxa are likely to have frequencies that inversely correlate with sample DNA concentration and (2) sequences from contaminating taxa are likely to have higher prevalence in control samples than in true samples.

span.label: because the frequency method reads low sample concentration as evidence of contamination, any real sequence that is genuinely commoner in low-biomass samples presents with the contaminant signature - so mixing environments manufactures false positives out of true biology
span.quote: The assumptions of decontam, especially the frequency method, can be violated if bacterial biomass systematically differs between groups of samples. For example, if decontam were applied to a mixed set of stool (high biomass) and airway (low biomass) samples, real sequences in the airway samples could be classified as contaminants, because they have a higher frequency in the low-concentration samples.

span.label: decontam is not designed for cross-contamination, which violates its founding assumption that contaminants and true members are distinct populations
span.quote: Decontam assumes that contaminants and true community members are distinct from one another. This basic assumption is violated by cross-contamination—contaminant sequences arising from other processed samples.

span.label: the frequency method's approximations break down in exactly the low-biomass regime where contamination matters most - when contaminants are a large fraction of reads
span.quote: Frequency-based contaminant identification is not recommended for extremely low-biomass samples (C~S or C > S) because the simple approximations we are making for the dependence of contaminant frequency on total DNA concentration break down when contaminants comprise a large fraction of sequencing reads.

span.label: applying it across environments of systematically different biomass can classify real sequences as contaminants, because low concentration is the contaminant signature
span.quote: The assumptions of decontam, especially the frequency method, can be violated if bacterial biomass systematically differs between groups of samples. For example, if decontam were applied to a mixed set of stool (high biomass) and airway (low biomass) samples, real sequences in the airway samples could be classified as contaminants, because they have a higher frequency in the low-concentration samples.

span.label: it depends on patterns across samples, so it has low sensitivity for contaminants present in very few samples - the tail it cannot see
span.quote: Decontam depends on patterns across samples to identify contaminants and therefore has low sensitivity for detecting contaminants that are found in very few samples.

span.label: the default classification threshold is not recommended as-is: the authors direct users to read a threshold off their own score histogram instead
span.quote: The default classification threshold is P* = 0.1, but we highly recommend that users inspect the distribution of scores in their data and consider adjusting P* based on specific dataset characteristics

span.label: the method is less effective when groups of samples carry systematically different contaminant patterns, which is why batches must be declared by the user rather than detected
span.quote: Decontam uses patterns across samples to identify contaminants, but that approach can be less effective when groups of samples have systematically different contaminant patterns.

span.label: model comparison by ratio of sums-of-squared-residuals, carried from linear regression into a per-sequence classifier - and deliberately stripped of the inferential guarantee it carries in its home field
span.quote: The frequency-based score statistic is best thought of as a transformation that takes as input two values—the ratio of the sum-of-squared residuals, and the number of observations—and outputs a score that is a better classification statistic than the ratio of the sum-of-squared residuals alone.

span.label: a two-component mixture model, carried from statistical modelling to represent total DNA as contaminant plus sample
span.quote: Let total sample DNA (T) be a mixture of two components (T = C + S): contaminating DNA (C) present in uniform concentration across samples and true sample DNA (S) present in varying concentration across samples.

span.label: the field's standard check that a negative control shows no band on an agarose gel, taken as evidence that contamination is absent
span.note: eliminates: contamination in the sequencing library - and the paper's own sentence says this check does NOT eliminate it, because band-less samples still generate non-negligible reads · outcome: absent-stated-about-other
span.quote: Contamination is often assumed to be absent if control samples do not yield a band on an agarose gel. However, band-less samples can generate non-negligible numbers of sequencing reads, suggesting that gel-based quality control is insufficient.

span.label: removing every sequence that appears in a negative control
span.note: eliminates: contaminant sequences - and it OVER-removes, because cross-contamination puts abundant TRUE sequences into the negative controls · outcome: absent-stated-about-other
span.quote: Another approach is the removal of sequences that appear in negative controls (e.g.,). However, cross-contamination between samples often causes abundant true sequences to be detected in negative controls.

span.label: discarding sequences below an ad hoc relative abundance threshold
span.note: eliminates: abundant contaminants, which it fails to remove, while removing rare features that are truly present in the sample · outcome: absent-stated-about-other
span.quote: However, relative abundance thresholds remove rare features truly present in the sample and do not remove abundant contaminants that are the most likely to interfere with subsequent analysis.

span.label: excluding taxa on a blacklist of previously reported contaminants
span.note: eliminates: previously reported contaminants - leaving study-specific contaminants in place and removing true sequences · outcome: absent-stated-about-other
span.quote: Finally, “blacklist” methods exclude sequences or taxa previously identified as contaminants, but do not identify study-specific contaminants and often remove true sequences.

span.label: cross-checking taxonomic assignments against a second controlled vocabulary, HOMD against SILVA, at the genus level
span.note: eliminates: a contaminant call that is an artefact of one reference vocabulary's genus boundaries · outcome: partial
span.quote: We compared SILVA and HOMD classifications at the genus level, and we resolved assignments for the 80 sequences on which SILVA and HOMD disagreed by NCBI BLAST results.

span.label: an explicit `ambiguous` class for genera that neither reference database resolves, instead of forcing every genus into contaminant or oral
span.note: eliminates: a genus with no evidence either way being forced into `contaminant` or `oral` and counted as if it had been decided · outcome: held
span.quote: Genera were categorized into three groups by comparison to the oral and contamination databases: contaminant, if present in the contamination database and not in the oral database; oral, if present in the oral database and not in the contamination database; and ambiguous otherwise.

span.label: turning the method on a published low-biomass claim - the placenta microbiome - where the expected answer was already contested
span.note: eliminates: a decontamination method validated only on data where the right answer was chosen by the people validating it · outcome: held
span.quote: The application of decontam to 16S rRNA gene sequencing data generated from placenta biopsies corroborated the conclusion that the data did not support the existence of a placenta microbiome.

span.label: contaminants
span.quote: However, the accuracy of marker-gene and metagenomic sequencing (MGS) is limited in practice by several processes that introduce contaminants—DNA sequences not truly present in the sampled community.

span.label: External contamination
span.quote: There are two major types of contaminants in MGS experiments that arise from different sources. External contamination is contributed from outside the samples being measured, with potential sources that include research subjects’ or investigators’ bodies, laboratory surfaces and air, and, perhaps most importantly, sample collection instruments and laboratory reagents. Internal or cross-contamination arises when samples mix with each other during sample processing or sequencing.

span.label: cross-contamination
span.quote: Decontam is not intended to detect cross-contamination, which presents with qualitatively different statistical patterns in MGS data.

span.label: score statistic
span.quote: Although inspired by the general linear F test, the frequency-based score statistic is not a p value, i.e., it is not associated with any guarantees on the type 1 error rate.

span.label: p value
span.quote: Although inspired by the general linear F test, the frequency-based score statistic is not a p value, i.e., it is not associated with any guarantees on the type 1 error rate.

span.label: classification threshold
span.quote: The default classification threshold is P* = 0.1, but we highly recommend that users inspect the distribution of scores in their data and consider adjusting P* based on specific dataset characteristics

span.label: negative controls
span.quote: Another approach is the removal of sequences that appear in negative controls (e.g.,). However, cross-contamination between samples often causes abundant true sequences to be detected in negative controls.

span.label: gel-based quality control
span.quote: Contamination is often assumed to be absent if control samples do not yield a band on an agarose gel. However, band-less samples can generate non-negligible numbers of sequencing reads, suggesting that gel-based quality control is insufficient.

span.label: relative abundance thresholds
span.quote: However, relative abundance thresholds remove rare features truly present in the sample and do not remove abundant contaminants that are the most likely to interfere with subsequent analysis.

span.label: true community members
span.quote: Decontam assumes that contaminants and true community members are distinct from one another. This basic assumption is violated by cross-contamination—contaminant sequences arising from other processed samples.

span.label: low-biomass
span.quote: Frequency-based contaminant identification is not recommended for extremely low-biomass samples (C~S or C > S) because the simple approximations we are making for the dependence of contaminant frequency on total DNA concentration break down when contaminants comprise a large fraction of sequencing reads.

span.label: SILVA
span.quote: We compared SILVA and HOMD classifications at the genus level, and we resolved assignments for the 80 sequences on which SILVA and HOMD disagreed by NCBI BLAST results.

span.label: HOMD
span.quote: We compared SILVA and HOMD classifications at the genus level, and we resolved assignments for the 80 sequences on which SILVA and HOMD disagreed by NCBI BLAST results.

span.label: processing batches
span.quote: Decontam allows the user to specify processing batches, in which case score statistics are generated from each batch independently and then combined in a user-selectable fashion for classification

span.label: placenta microbiome
span.quote: The application of decontam to 16S rRNA gene sequencing data generated from placenta biopsies corroborated the conclusion that the data did not support the existence of a placenta microbiome.

span.label: score statistic P - AS COMPUTED: set equal to a p-value from the chi-square or Fisher's exact test, and so arithmetically indistinguishable from one
span.quote: Although the prevalence-based score statistic is set equal to a p-value from the chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests, it is used by decontam only as a score that effectively distinguishes between the contaminant and non-contaminant mixture components.

span.label: score statistic P - AS LICENSED: a classification score only, explicitly carrying no guarantee on the type 1 error rate. The paper states the difference rather than leaving it to the reader
span.quote: Although inspired by the general linear F test, the frequency-based score statistic is not a p value, i.e., it is not associated with any guarantees on the type 1 error rate.

span.label: accuracy of decontam - PER SEQUENCE FEATURE: specificity and sensitivity described as sometimes moderate
span.quote: The sensitivity of contaminant identification increased substantially with feature prevalence. As a result, while the specificity and sensitivity of decontam on a per-feature basis were sometimes moderate, accuracy evaluated on a per-read basis reached exceptional levels.

span.label: accuracy of decontam - PER READ: described as reaching exceptional levels, on the same classifications of the same data. The unit of account decides which number is reported
span.quote: The sensitivity of contaminant identification increased substantially with feature prevalence. As a result, while the specificity and sensitivity of decontam on a per-feature basis were sometimes moderate, accuracy evaluated on a per-read basis reached exceptional levels.

span.label: critiques → gel-band quality control as evidence that a sequencing run is free of contamination
span.quote: Contamination is often assumed to be absent if control samples do not yield a band on an agarose gel. However, band-less samples can generate non-negligible numbers of sequencing reads, suggesting that gel-based quality control is insufficient.

span.label: critiques → ad hoc in silico decontamination - abundance thresholds, negative-control subtraction and contaminant blacklists
span.quote: However, relative abundance thresholds remove rare features truly present in the sample and do not remove abundant contaminants that are the most likely to interfere with subsequent analysis.

span.label: builds-on → prior reports of the two contaminant signatures: inverse correlation with DNA concentration, and presence in negative controls
span.quote: Decontam implements two simple de novo classification methods based on widely reproduced signatures of external contamination: (1) Sequences from contaminating taxa are likely to have frequencies that inversely correlate with sample DNA concentration and (2) sequences from contaminating taxa are likely to have higher prevalence in control samples than in true samples.

span.label: confirms → the conclusion that marker-gene data from placenta biopsies do not support an indigenous placenta microbiome
span.quote: The application of decontam to 16S rRNA gene sequencing data generated from placenta biopsies corroborated the conclusion that the data did not support the existence of a placenta microbiome.

span.label: score statistic —distinct-from→ p value
span.note: differs in: whether it licenses a claim about the type 1 error rate · the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.95
span.quote: Although inspired by the general linear F test, the frequency-based score statistic is not a p value, i.e., it is not associated with any guarantees on the type 1 error rate.

span.label: contaminants —distinct-from→ true community members
span.note: differs in: whether the sequence originated in the sampled environment · the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: Decontam assumes that contaminants and true community members are distinct from one another. This basic assumption is violated by cross-contamination—contaminant sequences arising from other processed samples.

span.label: cross-contamination —distinct-from→ External contamination
span.note: differs in: whether the contaminating DNA came from outside the study or from another sample in it · the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: There are two major types of contaminants in MGS experiments that arise from different sources. External contamination is contributed from outside the samples being measured, with potential sources that include research subjects’ or investigators’ bodies, laboratory surfaces and air, and, perhaps most importantly, sample collection instruments and laboratory reagents. Internal or cross-contamination arises when samples mix with each other during sample processing or sequencing.

span.label: the score decontam reports is computed as a tail probability and is explicitly not a p value - it carries no type 1 error guarantee
span.term: the score decontam reports is computed as a tail probability and is explicitly not a p value - it carries no type 1 error guarantee
span.quote: Although inspired by the general linear F test, the frequency-based score statistic is not a p value, i.e., it is not associated with any guarantees on the type 1 error rate.

span.label: the same classifications are 'sometimes moderate' per sequence feature and 'exceptional' per read - the unit of account decides the number
span.term: the same classifications are 'sometimes moderate' per sequence feature and 'exceptional' per read - the unit of account decides the number
span.quote: The sensitivity of contaminant identification increased substantially with feature prevalence. As a result, while the specificity and sensitivity of decontam on a per-feature basis were sometimes moderate, accuracy evaluated on a per-read basis reached exceptional levels.

span.label: the field's usual contamination control - no band on a gel - does not work, because band-less samples still generate substantial reads
span.term: the field's usual contamination control - no band on a gel - does not work, because band-less samples still generate substantial reads
span.quote: Contamination is often assumed to be absent if control samples do not yield a band on an agarose gel. However, band-less samples can generate non-negligible numbers of sequencing reads, suggesting that gel-based quality control is insufficient.

span.label: two curated taxonomic databases disagreed on 80 sequences and the disagreement had to be settled by a third method
span.term: two curated taxonomic databases disagreed on 80 sequences and the disagreement had to be settled by a third method
span.quote: We compared SILVA and HOMD classifications at the genus level, and we resolved assignments for the 80 sequences on which SILVA and HOMD disagreed by NCBI BLAST results.

span.label: contamination biases hardest in low-biomass environments, which is exactly where the frequency method's assumptions break down
span.term: contamination biases hardest in low-biomass environments, which is exactly where the frequency method's assumptions break down
span.quote: Frequency-based contaminant identification is not recommended for extremely low-biomass samples (C~S or C > S) because the simple approximations we are making for the dependence of contaminant frequency on total DNA concentration break down when contaminants comprise a large fraction of sequencing reads.

span.label: DNA sequences not truly present in the sampled community - a definition by provenance, so nothing in the sequence itself can settle it
span.quote: However, the accuracy of marker-gene and metagenomic sequencing (MGS) is limited in practice by several processes that introduce contaminants—DNA sequences not truly present in the sampled community.

span.label: contributed from outside the samples being measured; distinguished from internal or cross-contamination, which arises when samples mix with each other
span.quote: There are two major types of contaminants in MGS experiments that arise from different sources. External contamination is contributed from outside the samples being measured, with potential sources that include research subjects’ or investigators’ bodies, laboratory surfaces and air, and, perhaps most importantly, sample collection instruments and laboratory reagents. Internal or cross-contamination arises when samples mix with each other during sample processing or sequencing.

span.label: a transformation taking the ratio of sums-of-squared residuals and the number of observations, and returning a better classification statistic than the ratio alone - explicitly not a p value
span.quote: The frequency-based score statistic is best thought of as a transformation that takes as input two values—the ratio of the sum-of-squared residuals, and the number of observations—and outputs a score that is a better classification statistic than the ratio of the sum-of-squared residuals alone.

span.label: the default classification threshold, which the authors recommend against using unexamined
span.quote: The default classification threshold is P* = 0.1, but we highly recommend that users inspect the distribution of scores in their data and consider adjusting P* based on specific dataset characteristics

span.label: the threshold at which classification reduces to 'is the contaminant model the better fit'
span.quote: The threshold P* = 0.5 has a particularly simple interpretation: In the frequency approach, sequence features would be classified as contaminants if the contaminant model is a better fit than the non-contaminant model, and in the prevalence approach, sequence features would be classified as contaminants if present in a higher fraction of negative controls than true samples.

span.label: sequences on which the two reference databases disagreed, resolved by BLAST
span.quote: We compared SILVA and HOMD classifications at the genus level, and we resolved assignments for the 80 sequences on which SILVA and HOMD disagreed by NCBI BLAST results.

span.label: general linear F test
span.quote: Although inspired by the general linear F test, the frequency-based score statistic is not a p value, i.e., it is not associated with any guarantees on the type 1 error rate.

span.label: type 1 error rate
span.quote: Although inspired by the general linear F test, the frequency-based score statistic is not a p value, i.e., it is not associated with any guarantees on the type 1 error rate.

span.label: chi-square
span.quote: Although the prevalence-based score statistic is set equal to a p-value from the chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests, it is used by decontam only as a score that effectively distinguishes between the contaminant and non-contaminant mixture components.

span.label: Fisher’s exact tests
span.quote: Although the prevalence-based score statistic is set equal to a p-value from the chi-square or Fisher’s exact tests, it is used by decontam only as a score that effectively distinguishes between the contaminant and non-contaminant mixture components.

span.label: specificity
span.quote: The sensitivity of contaminant identification increased substantially with feature prevalence. As a result, while the specificity and sensitivity of decontam on a per-feature basis were sometimes moderate, accuracy evaluated on a per-read basis reached exceptional levels.

span.label: sensitivity
span.quote: The sensitivity of contaminant identification increased substantially with feature prevalence. As a result, while the specificity and sensitivity of decontam on a per-feature basis were sometimes moderate, accuracy evaluated on a per-read basis reached exceptional levels.

span.label: sample DNA concentration
span.quote: Decontam implements two simple de novo classification methods based on widely reproduced signatures of external contamination: (1) Sequences from contaminating taxa are likely to have frequencies that inversely correlate with sample DNA concentration and (2) sequences from contaminating taxa are likely to have higher prevalence in control samples than in true samples.

span.quote: Decontam implements two simple de novo classification methods based on widely reproduced signatures of external contamination: (1) Sequences from contaminating taxa are likely to have frequencies that inversely correlate with sample DNA concentration and (2) sequences from contaminating taxa are likely to have higher prevalence in control samples than in true samples.
